name: Angelo Clareno
knownFor: A leader of the Franciscan Spirituals, the friars who wanted the Rule of Francis kept to the letter. He was jailed in Italy, exiled to Greece and questioned at Avignon by Pope John XXII, and defended his brothers as no heretics. His commentary on the Rule and his letter of defense survive. Franz Ehrle judged him the most likely writer of the History of the Seven Tribulations.
dates: No witness gives his birth year. Livarius Oliger, his 1912 editor, places his entry to the order about 1270, against older writers' 1260. Oliger and Ehrle date the hearing at Avignon to about 1317. He died on 15 June 1337 at the hermitage of Santa Maria de Aspro, Oliger and Ehrle say. Ehrle reckoned the year from a weekday in a note on his miracles. Older writers had said 1348.
place: The March of Ancona, where Oliger says he came from, Cingoli or Fossombrone. Cilician Armenia, as a missionary. Greece, where the brothers lived about 1295 to 1305, first on an island Ehrle names as Trixonia. Avignon, where he was questioned. Subiaco, where he lived after 1318. The hermitage of Santa Maria de Aspro in the Basilicata, where he died.
role: Franciscan friar, never a priest by his own words; leader of the Spirituals after Liberatus; writer and translator

keyWorks.title: Expositio Regulae Fratrum Minorum (commentary on the Rule of the Friars Minor)
keyWorks.about: written for a brother Thomas, to set out what Francis meant in the Rule. Oliger, who first printed it in 1912, dates it between 1321 and 1323. He notes that the later letters are far harsher in judging men and things.

keyWorks.title: Letter of defense (Epistola excusatoria)
keyWorks.about: written to John XXII to win his release, printed in full by Franz Ehrle in 1885. He writes that his brothers are no heretics, unless it is heresy to keep humbly what Francis believed about his Rule.

keyWorks.title: History of the Seven Tribulations of the Order of Friars Minor
keyWorks.about: a chronicle of the trials of the friars who held to strict poverty. It names no author. Ehrle printed it in part in 1886 and argued for Angelo; Döllinger also printed an extract. It tells the hearing at Avignon.

traces: Matthaeus Rader, introducing his own Latin John Climacus, calls Angelo the first of all Climacus's translators. He reports that Ambrose of Camaldoli found that version obscure, word for word.

His letters survive in one Florence manuscript, the Book of Letters of blessed Angelo of Clarino. Oliger thinks Simon Fidati of Cascia probably gathered them, and Simon wrote that he did not want his memory to perish.
A congregation called the Clareni was placed under the Friars Minor in 1472. Oliger says it is not yet fully settled whether it came down from him.
remembered: Simon Fidati of Cascia mourned him in a lament, as an angel in name and more truly in deed.
Bartholomew of Pisa, a Franciscan, calls him a remarkable preacher. Luke Wadding writes that he lived a most holy life in the order.
Oliger notes that the old Bollandists printed his acts and miracles under 15 June, though his cult was never approved by the church.
Paulinus of Venice, a Franciscan bishop hostile to the Spirituals, wrote that he called himself Angelo because he pretended to have angelic revelations.
Henry Charles Lea calls him "a man of the firmest and gentlest spirit".

uncertain: Who wrote the History of the Seven Tribulations. The work names no author. Franz Ehrle argued in 1886 and 1887 that Angelo was by far the most likely writer, and Conrad Eubel and Oliger follow him. Affò, an eighteenth-century writer, asked on what ground Wadding gave it to Angelo, and Ehrle reports doubts from Richard and from Tocco.
When he was born, and where. No witness gives his birth year. Oliger names Cingoli and Fossombrone, and thinks Fossombrone is more commonly and perhaps more rightly held.
When he joined the order. Ehrle placed it not long after 1260. Oliger rejects 1260, since Angelo would then have kept the Rule for seventy-seven years, and concludes about 1270.

When the Avignon hearing and the letter of defense took place. Ehrle dates the letter to the summer of 1317. Annibali da Latera, after Wadding, put it at the end of 1318 or early 1319. Eubel has the leaders summoned at the end of 1316 or early 1317.
Whether the 1334 arrest order was aimed at him. The bull does not name the heretic who called himself head of the Fraticelli. Eubel adds Angelo's name in brackets.

When he died. Ehrle fixed 1337 from a note that the scribe helped on a Friday in the Pentecost octave, the feast of St Anthony. That weekday fell on 13 June only in 1317, 1337 and 1348. Older writers gave 1348.
